cap: Each congenital infection leaves one finding that names it. Calcifications split the two brain invaders: diffuse in toxoplasmosis, periventricular in cytomegalovirus. Cataracts with a patent ductus arteriosus mean rubella, hydrops means parvovirus B19, limb hypoplasia with zigzag scars means varicella, and saber shins with Hutchinson teeth mean late congenital syphilis.
teach: Pair each maternal clue with its organism: cat litter or undercooked meat for Toxoplasma; the saliva and urine of young children for cytomegalovirus; a school-age child with slapped-cheek rash for parvovirus B19; an unvaccinated mother with rash and joint pain for rubella; genital lesions at delivery for herpes simplex; and travel to, or a partner from, an area with Zika virus for microcephaly. A blueberry-muffin rash, made by extramedullary hematopoiesis in the skin, occurs with both rubella and cytomegalovirus, so it never settles the organism by itself. Parvovirus B19 causes hydrops by destroying erythroid progenitor cells, so the fetus becomes anemic and develops high-output heart failure.
